--- title: "Matrix Algebra for Regression" subtitle: "How a regression model is written, and solved, with vectors and matrices." description: "The design matrix, the normal equations, solving for the coefficients with matrix operations in R, and what multicollinearity does to them." order: 3 unit: "Foundations" categories: [Foundations] --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"} ## Learning objectives By the end of this lecture, you will be able to: - Understand why regression requires matrix algebra - Recognize the matrix form of regression: **Y = Xβ** - Calculate regression coefficients using **β = (X'X)^(-1)X'Y** - Identify multicollinearity problems through singular matrices - Interpret error messages like "matrix is singular" - Apply these concepts to real public health regression problems ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(knitr) library(kableExtra) library(plotly) library(car) # For VIF library(NHANES) # Real US health survey data ``` ::: ## Why Matrix Algebra? A regression model is a system of linear equations in the unknown coefficients. Matrix algebra is the mathematical engine that allows regression analysis to **scale from a simple two-variable problem to complex models with thousands of predictors.** While you can calculate a simple linear regression using basic arithmetic, it **quickly becomes inefficient and visually cluttered as you add more variables.** Writing the whole system as matrices lets us: 1. Express the model in one compact line. 2. Derive the least‑squares solution in closed form (the normal equations). 3. Compute statistics (variance, covariance, predictions, influence) with matrix formulas. 4. Solve large problems efficiently with numerical linear‑algebra routines. Without matrices, a multiple linear regression equation for $n$ observations and $k$ predictors would look like a giant list of individual equations: $$y_1 = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{11} + \beta_2x_{12} + \dots + \beta_kx_{1k} + \epsilon_1$$ $$y_2 = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{21} + \beta_2x_{22} + \dots + \beta_kx_{2k} + \epsilon_2$$ $$\vdots$$ $$y_n = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{n1} + \beta_2x_{n2} + \dots + \beta_kx_{nk} + \epsilon_n$$ With matrix algebra, this entire system collapses into one elegant expression: $$\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}$$ Modern statistical software (like the survey or gtsummary packages you use in R) doesn't "think" in terms of individual data points. It uses highly optimized linear algebra libraries (like BLAS or LAPACK) to perform these matrix inversions and multiplications. This is what allows you to process large datasets with complex survey designs in seconds rather than hours. ## A Real Public Health Problem ### The Research Question **What factors predict systolic blood pressure in US adults, and how do they interact?** We need to control for multiple risk factors: - Age (blood pressure increases with age) - BMI (obesity is a major hypertension risk factor) - Physical activity (exercise lowers blood pressure) - Smoking status (affects cardiovascular health) **This is a multivariable problem** - we need regression, not just correlation! ### The Dataset: NHANES We'll use the **National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES)** - real data from US health surveys (the `NHANES` R package, 2009-2012). NHANES asks "Do you smoke now?" (`SmokeNow`) only of people who have smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their life (`Smoke100`). Everyone else has a missing `SmokeNow`, so we code people who never smoked 100 cigarettes as **not current smokers** rather than dropping them. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load and prepare NHANES data # Focus on adults (21+) with complete blood pressure and predictor data set.seed(553) # For reproducibility bp_data <- NHANES |> mutate( # Convert Yes/No to 1/0 for regression Physically_Active = ifelse(PhysActive == "Yes", 1, 0), # Never smoked 100 cigarettes = not a current smoker Current_Smoker = case_when( Smoke100 == "No" ~ 0, SmokeNow == "Yes" ~ 1, SmokeNow == "No" ~ 0 ) ) |> filter(Age >= 21, # Adults only !is.na(BPSysAve), # Must have BP measured !is.na(BMI), # Must have BMI !is.na(Physically_Active), # Physical activity status !is.na(Current_Smoker)) |> # Current smoking status select(ID, BPSysAve, Age, BMI, Physically_Active, Current_Smoker, Weight, Height) |> slice_sample(n = 200) |> # Random sample of 200 for clarity arrange(ID) # Display first 10 rows bp_data |> head(10) |> kable(caption = "NHANES Blood Pressure Study Data (First 10 Observations)", digits = 1) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: **What we're looking at:** BPSysAve is systolic blood pressure - values ≥140 mmHg indicate hypertension. ### Summary Statistics ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create a cleaner summary table bp_data |> select(-ID) |> summarise( across(everything(), list(Mean = ~round(mean(., na.rm = TRUE), 2), SD = ~round(sd(., na.rm = TRUE), 2), Min = ~round(min(., na.rm = TRUE), 1), Max = ~round(max(., na.rm = TRUE), 1)), .names = "{.col}_{.fn}") ) |> # Split "Physically_Active_Mean" at the last underscore only pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("Variable", "Statistic"), names_pattern = "(.*)_(Mean|SD|Min|Max)$", values_to = "Value") |> pivot_wider(names_from = Statistic, values_from = Value) |> kable(caption = "Summary Statistics of NHANES Blood Pressure Data") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

BP:", round(BPSysAve, 1), "mmHg", "

Active:", ifelse(Physically_Active==1, "Yes", "No")), type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers', marker = list(size = 8, opacity = 0.6)) |> layout(title = "BMI vs Systolic BP in NHANES (Interactive - hover for details)", xaxis = list(title = "Body Mass Index (kg/m²)"), yaxis = list(title = "Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: [Figure description: interactive scatter plot of systolic blood pressure against BMI for 200 NHANES adults. BMI runs from about 19 to 61 kg/m² and systolic pressure from about 80 to 182 mmHg. The 31 hypertensive readings (140 or higher) are red and sit at the top of the cloud across the whole BMI range; the correlation between BMI and systolic pressure is 0.01.]{.visually-hidden} **Question:** Is higher BMI associated with higher blood pressure? Or are other factors confounding this? **Answer:** We need **multiple regression** to control for age, physical activity, and smoking! ## The Regression Problem: Why We Need Matrices ### What We Want to Estimate We want to fit this model: $$\text{BP} = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{Age}) + \beta_2(\text{BMI}) + \beta_3(\text{Active}) + \beta_4(\text{Smoker}) + \epsilon$$ With 200 observations and 4 predictors, we have **200 equations** with **5 unknowns** (β₀, β₁, β₂, β₃, β₄). With illustrative values, they look like this: $$120 = \beta_0 + 35\beta_1 + 28.5\beta_2 + 1\beta_3 + 0\beta_4 + \epsilon_1$$ $$135 = \beta_0 + 52\beta_1 + 31.2\beta_2 + 0\beta_3 + 1\beta_4 + \epsilon_2$$ $$\vdots$$ $$115 = \beta_0 + 41\beta_1 + 24.8\beta_2 + 1\beta_3 + 0\beta_4 + \epsilon_{200}$$ **Writing this by hand is impossible!** **Solution:** Matrix algebra lets us write this compactly as **Y = Xβ** ## Matrix Notation for Regression ### The Compact Form Instead of 200 separate equations, we write: $$\underbrace{\mathbf{Y}}_{n \times 1} = \underbrace{\mathbf{X}}_{n \times (p+1)} \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{(p+1) \times 1} + \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{n \times 1}$$ Where: - **Y** = vector of outcomes (blood pressure values) - **X** = matrix of predictors (including intercept column) - **β** = vector of coefficients we want to estimate - **ε** = vector of errors ### What This Looks Like With Real Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create the Y vector (outcomes) Y <- bp_data$BPSysAve # Create the X matrix (predictors + intercept) X <- bp_data |> select(Age, BMI, Physically_Active, Current_Smoker) |> mutate(intercept = 1) |> select(intercept, everything()) |> as.matrix() # Show dimensions tibble( Matrix = c("Y (outcomes)", "X (predictors)", "β (coefficients)"), Dimensions = c( paste(length(Y), "× 1"), paste(nrow(X), "×", ncol(X)), paste(ncol(X), "× 1") ), Interpretation = c( "200 blood pressure measurements", "200 observations × 5 columns (1 intercept + 4 predictors)", "5 coefficients to estimate" ) ) |> kable(caption = "Matrix Dimensions for Regression") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Matrix Dimensions for Regression
Matrix Dimensions Interpretation
Y (outcomes) 200 × 1 200 blood pressure measurements
X (predictors) 200 × 5 200 observations × 5 columns (1 intercept + 4 predictors)
β (coefficients) 5 × 1 5 coefficients to estimate
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Show first 8 rows of X X[1:8, ] |> as.data.frame() |> kable(caption = "Design Matrix X (First 8 Rows)", digits = 1) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Design Matrix X (First 8 Rows)
intercept Age BMI Physically_Active Current_Smoker
1 45 27.2 1 0
1 56 19.7 1 0
1 66 28.6 0 0
1 70 40.5 0 1
1 46 34.7 0 1
1 60 30.7 1 0
1 57 31.9 1 0
1 48 35.5 0 0
````` ::: ::: **Key Point:** The first column of X is all 1's (for the intercept β₀), and our binary variables (Physically_Active, Current_Smoker) are coded as 0/1. In regression analysis, **the intercept ($\beta_0$) represents the expected value of your outcome variable (Blood Pressure) when all your predictors (Age, BMI, etc.) are equal to zero.** While "zero BMI" or "zero Age" isn't physically possible, the intercept provides the essential starting point or "baseline" for the mathematical model. Since the regression equation is solved by multiplying the X matrix by the $\beta$ vector, we include a column of 1s because When you perform the matrix multiplication $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}$, the first element of each row in $\mathbf{X}$ is multiplied by $\beta_0$. **By making that element 1, you ensure that $\beta_0$ is added to the predicted value exactly as it is ($\beta_0 \times 1 = \beta_0$).** ## Matrix Operations You Need to Know ### 1. Matrix Transpose (X') **When you need it:** Calculating X'X and X'Y for regression **What it does:** Flips rows and columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Small example with health data (first 3 NHANES participants) small_example <- X[1:3, ] rownames(small_example) <- paste("Person", 1:3) small_example |> kable(caption = "Original Matrix (People × Variables)", digits = 1) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Original Matrix (People × Variables)
intercept Age BMI Physically_Active Current_Smoker
Person 1 1 45 27.2 1 0
Person 2 1 56 19.7 1 0
Person 3 1 66 28.6 0 0
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} t(small_example) |> kable(caption = "Transposed Matrix (Variables × People)", digits = 1) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Transposed Matrix (Variables × People)
Person 1 Person 2 Person 3
intercept 1.0 1.0 1.0
Age 45.0 56.0 66.0
BMI 27.2 19.7 28.6
Physically_Active 1.0 1.0 0.0
Current_Smoker 0.0 0.0 0.0
````` ::: ::: **Why this matters:** X'X gives us sums of squares and cross-products we need for regression - notice how transposing flips the matrix so we can multiply X'X. ### 2. Matrix Multiplication (X'X) **When you need it:** This is the key step in calculating regression coefficients Let's look at the data with 200 observations in it (these values could be different depending on the random sample). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate X'X for our blood pressure data XtX <- t(X) %*% X XtX |> kable(caption = "X'X Matrix (Sum of Squares and Cross Products)", digits = 0) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
X'X Matrix (Sum of Squares and Cross Products)
intercept Age BMI Physically_Active Current_Smoker
intercept 200 10021 5955 105 29
Age 10021 564721 298474 5056 1225
BMI 5955 298474 186009 2988 861
Physically_Active 105 5056 2988 105 7
Current_Smoker 29 1225 861 7 29
````` ::: ::: **What do these numbers mean?** - **Diagonal:** Sum of squares for each variable - `XtX[2,2]` = Sum of (Age)² - `XtX[3,3]` = Sum of (BMI)² - **Off-diagonal:** Cross products between variables - `XtX[2,3]` = Sum of (Age × BMI) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Show what's in X'X tibble( Element = c("XtX[1,1]", "XtX[2,2]", "XtX[2,3]"), Calculation = c( "Sum of 1² (n observations)", "Sum of (Age)²", "Sum of (Age × BMI)" ), Value = c( XtX[1,1], XtX[2,2], XtX[2,3] ) ) |> kable(caption = "Interpreting X'X Elements", digits = 0) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Interpreting X'X Elements
Element Calculation Value
XtX[1,1] Sum of 1² (n observations) 200
XtX[2,2] Sum of (Age)² 564721
XtX[2,3] Sum of (Age × BMI) 298474
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Verify one calculation tibble( Method = c("From X'X", "Manual calculation"), Result = c( XtX[2,2], sum(bp_data$Age^2) ) ) |> kable(caption = "Verification: XtX[2,2] = Sum of (Age)²") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Verification: XtX[2,2] = Sum of (Age)²
Method Result
From X'X 564721
Manual calculation 564721
````` ::: ::: **Interpretation:** The diagonal shows variability in each predictor, off-diagonal shows how predictors co-vary. ### 3. Matrix Inverse: (X'X)^(-1) **When you need it:** This is THE critical step for calculating β **What it does:** The matrix equivalent of division **Important:** Only works if X'X is **not singular** (determinant ≠ 0) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate the inverse XtX_inv <- solve(XtX) XtX_inv |> kable(caption = "(X'X)^(-1): The Inverse Matrix", digits = 6) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
(X'X)^(-1): The Inverse Matrix
intercept Age BMI Physically_Active Current_Smoker
intercept 0.189574 -0.000983 -0.003901 -0.029565 -0.025053
Age -0.000983 0.000017 0.000002 0.000106 0.000192
BMI -0.003901 0.000002 0.000121 0.000368 0.000148
Physically_Active -0.029565 0.000106 0.000368 0.022932 0.008615
Current_Smoker -0.025053 0.000192 0.000148 0.008615 0.044966
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Verify: X'X × (X'X)^(-1) should equal the identity matrix verification <- XtX %*% XtX_inv verification |> round(10) |> # Round to avoid floating point display issues kable(caption = "Verification: X'X × (X'X)^(-1) = I (Identity Matrix)") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Verification: X'X × (X'X)^(-1) = I (Identity Matrix)
intercept Age BMI Physically_Active Current_Smoker
intercept 1 0 0 0 0
Age 0 1 0 0 0
BMI 0 0 1 0 0
Physically_Active 0 0 0 1 0
Current_Smoker 0 0 0 0 1
````` ::: ::: **The identity matrix** has 1's on diagonal, 0's elsewhere - it's like multiplying by 1! ## The Magic Formula: Calculating Beta ### The Normal Equations Starting from **Y = Xβ**, we derive: $$\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Y}$$ **This is how R calculates regression coefficients in `lm()`!** ### Step-by-Step Calculation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Step 1: Calculate X'Y XtY <- t(X) %*% Y data.frame( Component = c("X'Y"), Dimensions = paste(nrow(XtY), "× 1"), Interpretation = "Cross products of predictors with outcome" ) |> kable(caption = "Step 1: Calculate X'Y") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Step 1: Calculate X'Y
Component Dimensions Interpretation
X'Y 5 × 1 Cross products of predictors with outcome
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} XtY |> as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("Variable") |> rename(Value = V1) |> kable(caption = "X'Y Values", digits = 0) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
X'Y Values
Variable Value
intercept 24452
Age 1241710
BMI 728270
Physically_Active 12656
Current_Smoker 3524
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Step 2: Calculate beta = (X'X)^(-1) × X'Y beta_hat <- XtX_inv %*% XtY ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Estimated Regression Coefficients (Manual Matrix Calculation)
Coefficient Estimate Interpretation
β₀ (Intercept) 111.23 Baseline systolic BP (mmHg)
β₁ (Age) 0.26 Change per 1 year increase in age
β₂ (BMI) -0.02 Change per 1 unit increase in BMI
β₃ (Physically Active) -2.53 Difference for physically active individuals
β₄ (Current Smoker) 0.67 Difference for current smokers
````` ::: ::: ### Verification with lm() Does our manual matrix calculation match R's `lm()`? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Fit the same model using lm() model <- lm(BPSysAve ~ Age + BMI + Physically_Active + Current_Smoker, data = bp_data) # Compare results comparison <- data.frame( Coefficient = c("Intercept", "Age", "BMI", "Physically_Active", "Current_Smoker"), Matrix_Calculation = as.vector(beta_hat), lm_Function = coef(model) ) comparison |> kable(caption = "Comparison: Manual vs lm()", digits = 4) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Comparison: Manual vs lm()
Coefficient Matrix_Calculation lm_Function
(Intercept) Intercept 111.2289 111.2289
Age Age 0.2584 0.2584
BMI BMI -0.0230 -0.0230
Physically_Active Physically_Active -2.5270 -2.5270
Current_Smoker Current_Smoker 0.6672 0.6672
````` ::: ::: **They match perfectly!** This proves that `lm()` uses the matrix formula β = (X'X)^(-1)X'Y internally. ## Interpreting the Results ### What Do These Coefficients Tell Us? ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Clinical Interpretation of Regression Coefficients
Predictor Effect p_value Meaning
Age +0.26 mmHg <0.001 BP is higher with each additional year of age (statistically significant)
BMI -0.02 mmHg 0.90 No clear association with each 1-unit higher BMI (not statistically significant)
Physically Active -2.53 mmHg 0.31 No clear association with being physically active (not statistically significant)
Current Smoker +0.67 mmHg 0.85 No clear association with being a current smoker (not statistically significant)
````` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: [Figure description: interactive dot plot of the four regression coefficients with standard-error bars. Age +0.26 (SE 0.07), BMI -0.02 (SE 0.18), physically active -2.53 (SE 2.49), current smoker +0.67 (SE 3.48) mmHg. The two binary predictors have much wider bars than age and BMI.]{.visually-hidden} **Key finding:** Each additional year of age is associated with a 0.26 mmHg increase in systolic BP, controlling for the other factors (p < 0.001). Because age is measured in years, its coefficient looks small, but over 30 years it adds up to about 8 mmHg. ### Predicted vs Observed ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Add predictions to data bp_data$predicted <- as.vector(X %*% beta_hat) bp_data$residual <- bp_data$BPSysAve - bp_data$predicted # Interactive plot plot_ly(bp_data, x = ~predicted, y = ~BPSysAve, color = ~BP_Status, colors = c("Hypertensive" = "red", "Normal" = "steelblue"), text = ~paste("ID:", ID, "
Observed BP:", round(BPSysAve, 1), "mmHg", "
Predicted:", round(predicted, 1), "mmHg", "
Residual:", round(residual, 1), "
Status:", BP_Status), type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers', marker = list(size = 8, opacity = 0.6)) |> add_trace(x = c(min(bp_data$predicted), max(bp_data$predicted)), y = c(min(bp_data$predicted), max(bp_data$predicted)), type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines', line = list(color = 'black', dash = 'dash'), name = 'Perfect Prediction', showlegend = TRUE, inherit = FALSE) |> layout(title = "Predicted vs Observed Systolic BP", xaxis = list(title = "Predicted Systolic BP (mmHg)"), yaxis = list(title = "Observed Systolic BP (mmHg)")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: [Figure description: interactive scatter plot of observed against predicted systolic blood pressure, with a dashed diagonal line for perfect prediction. Predictions span only about 113 to 131 mmHg while observed values span 80 to 182 mmHg, so most points sit well above or below the line; the model explains 8% of the variation (R² = 0.08).]{.visually-hidden} **Points close to the diagonal line** are well-predicted by our model; **points far from the line** have large residuals (prediction errors). ## When Things Go Wrong: Multicollinearity ### What is Multicollinearity? **Multicollinearity** = When predictor variables are highly correlated with each other **Why it matters:** If one predictor is an exact combination of others (perfect collinearity), X'X is **singular** (non-invertible) and β cannot be calculated at all. If predictors are strongly but not perfectly related, X'X is **nearly singular**: β can be calculated, but small changes in the data move it a lot, and the standard errors grow. ### Real Example: The Redundant Variable Problem Let's try to include both **Weight** and **BMI** as predictors. Problem: BMI is calculated FROM weight and height! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Check if we have the variables needed bp_data_check <- bp_data |> filter(!is.na(Weight), !is.na(Height)) # BMI is weight(kg) / height(m)² # Since we already have BMI, let's show the relationship cor_check <- cor(bp_data_check[, c("Weight", "BMI", "Height")], use = "complete.obs") cor_check |> kable(caption = "Correlation Matrix: Weight, BMI, and Height", digits = 3) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Correlation Matrix: Weight, BMI, and Height
Weight BMI Height
Weight 1.000 0.853 0.456
BMI 0.853 1.000 -0.061
Height 0.456 -0.061 1.000
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Try to fit regression with both Weight and BMI X_bad <- bp_data_check |> select(Age, BMI, Weight, Physically_Active, Current_Smoker) |> mutate(intercept = 1) |> select(intercept, everything()) |> as.matrix() # What happens to X'X? XtX_bad <- t(X_bad) %*% X_bad # How close to singular? The condition number (largest / smallest # eigenvalue) grows as predictors become closer to linear combinations of # each other. We compute it on the predictors' correlation matrix so the # units of the variables do not matter (the determinant of X'X does depend # on units, which makes it a poor guide). cond_good <- kappa(cor(X[, -1]), exact = TRUE) cond_bad <- kappa(cor(X_bad[, -1]), exact = TRUE) data.frame( Predictors = c("Age, BMI, Active, Smoker", "Age, BMI, Weight, Active, Smoker"), Condition_number = round(c(cond_good, cond_bad), 1) ) |> kable(caption = "Adding Weight makes X'X much closer to singular") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Adding Weight makes X'X much closer to singular
Predictors Condition_number
Age, BMI, Active, Smoker 2.2
Age, BMI, Weight, Active, Smoker 14.0
````` ::: ::: **The issue:** Weight and BMI are highly correlated (r = 0.85). Adding Weight raises the condition number of the predictors from 2.2 to 14, about 6 times larger: X'X is closer to singular, though still far from the values (in the hundreds or thousands) that make inversion numerically unreliable. ### What Happens When You Try? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Fit with lm(): it runs without complaint, so look at the standard errors model_bad <- lm(BPSysAve ~ Age + BMI + Weight + Physically_Active + Current_Smoker, data = bp_data_check) tibble(Variable = names(coef(model_bad)), Coefficient = coef(model_bad)) |> kable(caption = "lm() Output with Both BMI and Weight", digits = 4) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
lm() Output with Both BMI and Weight
Variable Coefficient
(Intercept) 110.1704
Age 0.2733
BMI -0.6148
Weight 0.2155
Physically_Active -3.2104
Current_Smoker 0.2369
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Check standard errors - they'll be inflated! summary(model_bad)$coefficients |> as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("Variable") |> select(Variable, Estimate, `Std. Error`) |> kable(caption = "Notice the Large Standard Errors!", digits = 4) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

The standard error for BMI is 0.18 in the original model and 0.35 once Weight is added (1.9 times larger). That loss of precision is what multicollinearity does. ### Diagnosing Multicollinearity with VIF ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Check VIF (Variance Inflation Factor) for the problematic model vif_values <- vif(model_bad) data.frame( Variable = names(vif_values), VIF = vif_values, Problem = ifelse(vif_values > 5, "High (above 5)", "Below 5") ) |> kable(caption = "Variance Inflation Factors (VIF > 5 indicates multicollinearity)", digits = 2) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Here the VIFs for BMI and Weight are 4 and 3.8 (the variance of each estimate is that many times larger than it would be with uncorrelated predictors), compared with 1.1 for BMI without Weight. That is clearly inflated but still under the usual cutoff of 5: BMI and Weight are strongly related, yet Height gives Weight information that BMI does not, so they are not fully redundant. Cutoffs are guides, not tests. ## Practical Takeaways for Your Research ### When You'll Use This ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Calculate X'X (sum of squares and cross products) 2. Invert it (possible unless predictors are perfectly collinear) 3. Multiply by X'Y (cross products with outcome) ### Key Diagnostic: Check Your Correlation Matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Always check this before running regression! bp_data |> select(Age, BMI, Physically_Active, Current_Smoker) |> cor() |> kable(caption = "Predictor Correlation Matrix - Check Before Regression!", digits = 3) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
